A UBS report dated September 28, 2026, highlights that the S&P 500's forward P/E ratio has fallen 17% from its November peak, nearing the 20-30% declines typical of recessions. This drop coincides with a roughly 100-basis-point rise in the 10-year Treasury yield year-to-date, driven by a market shift from pricing rate cuts to pricing further hikes. Historical analysis shows the Federal Reserve's subsequent actions are crucial for equity direction.

The 10-year yield has reached 5.2%, significantly above its one-year moving average. In the past 40 years, it has breached 1.5 standard deviations above this average only seven times. In three instances (1994, 1999, 2022) where the Fed subsequently hiked rates over 100 basis points, the S&P 500 delivered negative or flat returns over the following year. In the other four episodes with mild or no hikes (2013, 2016, 2021, 2023), the index posted positive returns, averaging a 17.7% gain one year later.

Currently, markets price in about 88 bps of hikes over the next year, below the 100-bps threshold, suggesting a more moderate path is likely. Despite the P/E compression, which aligns with the 1994 cycle, UBS's valuation framework indicates the index trades at a ~21% discount to its implied P/E, supported by strong earnings growth and improved fundamentals.
